pages.text: One night, Ohenewaa stayed up much too late watching a film. In the morning, Mama called gently, “Wake up, Ohenewaa!” Her eyelids felt heavy, and she yawned all the way to school.
sentences: One night, Ohenewaa stayed up much too late watching a film.
In the morning, Mama called gently, “Wake up, Ohenewaa!” Her eyelids felt heavy, and she yawned all the way to school.
pages.alt: Sleepy little Ohenewaa in her lavender-and-yellow school dress rubbing her eyes and yawning wide as she walks along a sunny morning path beside Mama.

pages.text: In class, Ohenewaa could not remember the new letter sounds. When her friend leaned over to ask a question, Ohenewaa answered crossly, “Leave me alone!” Almost at once, she felt sorry.
sentences: In class, Ohenewaa could not remember the new letter sounds.
When her friend leaned over to ask a question, Ohenewaa answered crossly, “Leave me alone!” Almost at once, she felt sorry.
pages.alt: At a wooden classroom desk, tired Ohenewaa frowns with her chin in her hand while her classmate looks hurt beside her.

pages.text: Madam Salamatu knelt beside her desk and asked softly, “Did you sleep well last night?” Ohenewaa shook her head. “Sleep is when your body rests and grows,” said Madam Salamatu, “and when your brain stores what you have learned.”
sentences: Madam Salamatu knelt beside her desk and asked softly, “Did you sleep well last night?” Ohenewaa shook her head.
“Sleep is when your body rests and grows,” said Madam Salamatu, “and when your brain stores what you have learned.”
pages.alt: Kind Madam Salamatu kneeling beside Ohenewaa’s desk and speaking gently with a warm, reassuring smile.

pages.text: That evening, Ohenewaa and Mama planned a calm bedtime routine: eat supper early, switch screens off, wash, brush teeth, share a short story, and turn lights out at the same time each night. School-age children need about nine to twelve hours of sleep.
sentences: That evening, Ohenewaa and Mama planned a calm bedtime routine: eat supper early, switch screens off, wash, brush teeth, share a short story, and turn lights out at the same time each night.
School-age children need about nine to twelve hours of sleep.
pages.alt: Cosy Ghanaian bedroom at evening where Ohenewaa in soft yellow pyjamas sits happily on her bed while Mama reads a picture book beside a warm bedside lamp.

pages.text: The next morning, Ohenewaa woke up bright and refreshed. In class, she remembered her letter sounds and clapped happily as she sang with her friends. She felt cheerful and strong.
sentences: The next morning, Ohenewaa woke up bright and refreshed.
In class, she remembered her letter sounds and clapped happily as she sang with her friends.
pages.alt: Radiant, well-rested Ohenewaa clapping and singing joyfully alongside her smiling classmates in the bright morning classroom.

pages.text: After school, Ohenewaa hugged her little cousin and said, “A good sleep helps us learn, helps us grow, and helps us be kind.” Her cousin gave a big yawn. “Then I should go to bed early too!” Everyone laughed.

pages.alt: On the sunny family veranda, cheerful Ohenewaa hugs her yawning little cousin while Mama laughs warmly nearby.

activities.question: What does sleep help our body and brain do?
options: Rest, grow, and store what we learn

activities.question: What did Ohenewaa and Mama plan for the evening?
options: A calm bedtime routine at the same time each night

activities.prompt: Put Ohenewaa’s bedtime routine in order.
items: Eat supper early and switch screens off.

activities.prompt: How do you feel in the morning after a good night’s sleep?
